### Letter to John T. Stuart, 23 January 1841 (Abraham Lincoln primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Abraham Lincoln primary sources: Letter to John T. Stuart, 23 January 1841"]
Principle: Name your low state honestly to a trusted friend and hand off what you cannot carry.
- Situation: Lincoln, a 31-year-old Illinois legislator, answers his friend and former law partner Stuart about a congressional election and apologizes that the "deplorable state of my mind" will make the reply thin.
- He does the practical political report anyway, then tells Stuart plainly that he cannot give the usual news. He writes that he is "the most miserable man living" and that he cannot say whether he will ever be better.
- He says he fears he will be unable to attend to business and suggests a change of scene might help, then stops: he can write no more. He asks Stuart to adjust plans to his condition.
- Lesson: he told a friend the truth about his state, said what he could not do, and asked for a practical adjustment instead of pretending. This note describes the letter and does not diagnose him.

### Letter to Mary Speed, 27 September 1841 (Abraham Lincoln primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Abraham Lincoln primary sources: Letter to Mary Speed, 27 September 1841"]
Principle: Light company, small kindnesses and a little humor can lift a low season.
- Situation: eight months after his low winter, Lincoln writes from the road on the Illinois circuit to Mary Speed, the half-sister of his friend Joshua, after a long stay with the Speed family in Kentucky.
- The letter is warm, teasing and chatty. He recalls shared jokes, peaches and cream, and a badly pulled tooth, and asks after several people by name.
- He says a "present" from Mrs. Speed is, as she claims, the best cure for the "Blues" if one could take it according to the truth. He also observes, from a scene on a steamboat, that God "renders the worst of human conditions tolerable".
- Lesson: months after the January letter, his writing is light and social. The letter suggests company, a change of place and small pleasures, without claiming he was cured.

### Letter to Joshua Speed, 3 February 1842 (Abraham Lincoln primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Abraham Lincoln primary sources: Letter to Joshua Speed, 3 February 1842"]
Principle: Your distress can be real without being proof of what your fears say.
- Situation: Speed, tormented by doubts and fear for his fiancee's health, has written of his "excessively bad feeling". Lincoln replies from Springfield.
- Lincoln says he feels Speed's sorrows as keenly as his own, but reads the distress as evidence of Speed's love rather than its absence: a man who did not care would be calmly resigned.
- He acknowledges the cost to himself: "You know the Hell I have suffered on that point." He adds that he has been "quite clear of hypo" since Speed left, even better than the previous autumn, and he closes with village news and a request for a fast reply.
- Lesson: he speaks from his own scar, offers a reframe of the pain rather than a lecture, and reports his own improvement without claiming it is permanent.

### Letter to Joshua Speed, 13 February 1842 (Abraham Lincoln primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Abraham Lincoln primary sources: Letter to Joshua Speed, 13 February 1842"]
Principle: In despondency, remember it passes, and stay occupied rather than idle.
- Situation: Speed has just married after months of anguish. Lincoln writes days later, hoping his friend will need no more comfort but preparing him in case he does.
- He urges Speed, "as I have ever done", to remember even in the depth of despondency that he will shortly feel well again.
- He predicts Speed's nerves may fail him occasionally for a while before they settle, and suggests a practical step: if his mind is not right, do not be idle. Engage in some business or make preparations for it.
- Lesson: expect setbacks, hold onto the fact that low states end, and give the mind a task. He also admits the limits of his advice, since Speed is now on ground he has not occupied himself.

### Letter to Joshua Speed, 25 February 1842 (Abraham Lincoln primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Abraham Lincoln primary sources: Letter to Joshua Speed, 25 February 1842"]
Principle: Forebodings feel like knowledge but often are not; wait for the nerves to settle.
- Situation: Lincoln has waited anxiously for two letters from Speed and opens the second with "intense anxiety and trepidation", though it turns out better than he feared.
- He tells Speed their forebodings, "for which you and I are rather peculiar", are nonsense, and points to the evidence: Speed's second letter is plainly calmer than the first, at the very time Lincoln feared he would be worse.
- He suggests both men dream of an ideal far beyond anything earthly, so real life will fall short of the dream without being a failure. He passes on his father's saying about hugging a bad bargain tighter.
- Lesson: check dark predictions against the actual record, expect steadiness to come slowly, and do not measure a real life against an imagined perfect one.

### Letter to Joshua Speed, 4 July 1842 (Abraham Lincoln primary sources)
Cite as: [Source: "Abraham Lincoln primary sources: Letter to Joshua Speed, 4 July 1842"]
Principle: After a collapse, rebuild trust in yourself slowly and avoid big commitments meanwhile.
- Situation: five months after the crisis winter, Lincoln answers a delayed letter from Speed after weeks away on the legal circuit. The letter mixes friendship with debt-collection errands for Speed's business.
- He says the subject of his old trouble is still painful, and that silence from Speed or anyone cannot make him forget it.
- He explains what it cost: he had prized his ability to keep a resolution above every other trait, lost it, and has not yet regained it. Until he does, he says, he cannot trust himself in any matter of much importance.
- He steers by a scriptural line, "Stand still and see the salvation of the Lord", while noting he is poor and slips back in a month of idleness as much as he gains in a year. Lesson: recovery is measured in trust rebuilt, not the absence of pain, and it is honest to say it is unfinished.
